blocks.body:
What does the curve $5x^2 + 4xy + 2y^2 = 1$ look like? The cross term $4xy$ hides the answer. If we could rotate the coordinate axes so that the cross term disappears, we would see an ellipse with its axes along the new coordinate directions. The spectral theorem says that such a rotation always exists, for any number of variables, and that the right axes are the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix.

General matrices can fail to be diagonalisable, or have complex eigenvalues, or have eigenvectors at awkward angles. Symmetric matrices have none of these problems: their eigenvalues are real and their eigenvectors can be chosen perpendicular. This lesson proves that, using [[diagonalization]] and [[inner-products]], and shows what it buys.

blocks.title: Symmetric and self-adjoint
blocks.body:
A real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is symmetric if $A^{\mathsf T} = A$, that is $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$. With the dot product $\langle x, y\rangle = x^{\mathsf T}y$ this is equivalent to
$$\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \mathbb R^n,$$
since $\langle Ax, y\rangle = x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y$. A linear map with this property on an inner product space is called self-adjoint. A complex matrix with $\overline{A}^{\mathsf T} = A$ is called Hermitian; it is self-adjoint for $\langle x, y\rangle = \sum x_i\overline{y_i}$.

So a symmetric matrix is one that can be moved from one side of the inner product to the other.

blocks.title: The spectral theorem
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix. Then all eigenvalues of $A$ are real, and $\mathbb R^n$ has an orthonormal basis $q_1, \dots, q_n$ of eigenvectors of $A$. Equivalently, there are an orthogonal matrix $Q$ (with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$) and a real diagonal matrix $D$ with
$$A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}.$$
Conversely, every matrix of the form $QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $D$ real diagonal is symmetric. The analogous statement holds for complex Hermitian matrices, with $Q$ unitary ($\overline{Q}^{\mathsf T}Q = I$) and $D$ still real.

blocks.title: Two key facts
blocks.body:
The proof rests on two short observations.

Eigenvalues are real. Let $Av = \lambda v$ with $v \in \mathbb C^n$ nonzero (over $\mathbb C$ an eigenvalue always exists). Write $v^* = \overline{v}^{\mathsf T}$ and consider the number $s = v^*Av$. On the one hand $s = \lambda\, v^*v = \lambda\sum|v_i|^2$. On the other hand, since $A$ is real and symmetric, $\overline{s} = v^{\mathsf T}A\overline{v}$, and this $1\times 1$ matrix equals its own transpose $\overline{v}^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}v = v^*Av = s$. So $s$ is real, and $\lambda = s/\sum|v_i|^2$ is real. Then $A - \lambda I$ is a real singular matrix, so it also has a nonzero real vector in its kernel: real eigenvalues have real eigenvectors.

Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular. If $Av = \lambda v$ and $Aw = \mu w$ with $\lambda \ne \mu$, then
$$\lambda\langle v, w\rangle = \langle Av, w\rangle = \langle v, Aw\rangle = \mu\langle v, w\rangle,$$
so $(\lambda - \mu)\langle v, w\rangle = 0$ and $\langle v, w\rangle = 0$.

These two facts already prove the theorem when the eigenvalues are distinct: normalise one eigenvector for each eigenvalue. Repeated eigenvalues need an extra argument, because we must also show that each eigenspace is as large as the multiplicity. That is done by induction.

Proof of the spectral theorem. Induction on $n$; for $n = 1$ there is nothing to prove. Let $n \ge 2$. By the first key fact, $A$ has a real eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ with a real eigenvector, which we normalise to a unit vector $q_1$.

Let $W = q_1^{\perp} = \{w : \langle w, q_1\rangle = 0\}$, a subspace of dimension $n - 1$. The map $x \mapsto Ax$ sends $W$ into itself: if $w \in W$ then
$$\langle Aw, q_1\rangle = \langle w, Aq_1\rangle = \lambda_1\langle w, q_1\rangle = 0.$$
Choose an orthonormal basis $f_1, \dots, f_{n-1}$ of $W$ (Gram–Schmidt, see [[inner-products]]). The matrix $B$ of $A$ restricted to $W$ in this basis has entries $b_{ij} = \langle Af_j, f_i\rangle$, because coordinates in an orthonormal basis are inner products. Since $A$ is self-adjoint, $b_{ij} = \langle f_j, Af_i\rangle = b_{ji}$, so $B$ is a real symmetric $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix.

By the induction hypothesis, $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $B$. Translating coordinates back through $f_1, \dots, f_{n-1}$ (which preserves inner products), $W$ has an orthonormal basis $q_2, \dots, q_n$ of eigenvectors of $A$. Each of these is orthogonal to $q_1$, so $q_1, \dots, q_n$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$.

Finally let $Q$ have columns $q_1, \dots, q_n$ and $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$. Then $AQ = QD$ (column by column) and $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$ (orthonormality), so $A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. The converse is the computation $(QDQ^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = QD^{\mathsf T}Q^{\mathsf T} = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. The Hermitian case is the same proof with $\overline{\,\cdot\,}^{\mathsf T}$ in place of ${}^{\mathsf T}$.

blocks.title: Principal axes and quadratic forms
blocks.body:
Multiplying out $QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ column by row gives the spectral decomposition
$$A = \lambda_1q_1q_1^{\mathsf T} + \lambda_2q_2q_2^{\mathsf T} + \cdots + \lambda_nq_nq_n^{\mathsf T}.$$
Each $q_iq_i^{\mathsf T}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line through $q_i$ (it sends $x$ to $\langle x, q_i\rangle q_i$). So a symmetric matrix is a weighted sum of projections onto perpendicular lines: decompose $x$ along the axes $q_i$, stretch the $i$-th piece by $\lambda_i$, and add up. The unit sphere is mapped to an ellipsoid (flattened if some $\lambda_i = 0$) whose semi-axes point along the $q_i$ and have lengths $|\lambda_i|$.

The same decomposition simplifies quadratic forms. In the coordinates $y = Q^{\mathsf T}x$ (a rotation, possibly composed with a reflection),
$$x^{\mathsf T}Ax = x^{\mathsf T}QDQ^{\mathsf T}x = y^{\mathsf T}Dy = \lambda_1y_1^2 + \cdots + \lambda_ny_n^2,$$
and $\|y\| = \|x\|$. Two consequences follow at once.

- $A$ is positive definite ($x^{\mathsf T}Ax > 0$ for all $x \ne 0$) if and only if all its eigenvalues are positive.
- Rayleigh's principle: on the unit sphere, $x^{\mathsf T}Ax = \sum\lambda_iy_i^2$ with $\sum y_i^2 = 1$ is a weighted average of the eigenvalues. Hence
$$\lambda_{\min} \le x^{\mathsf T}Ax \le \lambda_{\max} \quad \text{for } \|x\| = 1,$$
with the maximum attained at a unit eigenvector for $\lambda_{\max}$ and the minimum at one for $\lambda_{\min}$.

blocks.title: Orthogonal diagonalisation with a repeated eigenvalue
blocks.body:
Find an orthogonal matrix $Q$ with $Q^{\mathsf T}AQ$ diagonal, where
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.$$
blocks.solution:
$A = I + J$ with $J$ the all-ones matrix, so (see [[eigen]]) the eigenvalues are $4$, with eigenvector $(1, 1, 1)$, and $1$, with eigenspace the plane $x + y + z = 0$.

The unit vector $q_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1)$ handles $\lambda = 4$. For $\lambda = 1$, any two independent vectors in the plane are eigenvectors, but they need not be orthogonal: $(1, -1, 0)$ and $(1, 0, -1)$ have inner product $1$. Apply Gram–Schmidt inside the eigenspace: $q_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$, then
$$(1, 0, -1) - \tfrac12(1, -1, 0) = \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, -1\right), \qquad q_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 1, -2).$$
With $Q = (q_1\ q_2\ q_3)$ we get $Q^{\mathsf T}AQ = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1, 1)$. The key point: eigenvectors for different eigenvalues came out orthogonal for free; within a repeated eigenvalue we had to orthogonalise by hand.

blocks.title: Principal axes of a conic
blocks.solution:
Write the left side as $x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ with $x = (x, y)$ and
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2\\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$$
(the cross coefficient $4$ is split equally between the two off-diagonal entries so that $A$ is symmetric). Here $\operatorname{tr} A = 7$ and $\det A = 6$, so the eigenvalues are $6$ and $1$. Solving $(A - 6I)v = 0$ gives $v = (2, 1)$; solving $(A - I)v = 0$ gives $v = (1, -2)$. These are orthogonal, as they must be.

In the rotated coordinates $u = \frac{2x + y}{\sqrt5}$, $w = \frac{x - 2y}{\sqrt5}$ the equation becomes
$$6u^2 + w^2 = 1,$$
an ellipse with semi-axis $\frac{1}{\sqrt6}$ in the direction $(2, 1)$ and semi-axis $1$ in the direction $(1, -2)$. Its area is $\pi\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\cdot 1 = \pi/\sqrt{\det A}$.

blocks.title: An inequality from the Rayleigh principle
blocks.body: Find the largest and smallest values of $xy + yz + zx$ over all real $x, y, z$ with $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$.
blocks.solution:
We have $xy + yz + zx = v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ for $v = (x, y, z)$ and
$$M = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac12(J - I).$$
$J$ has eigenvalues $3, 0, 0$, so $M$ has eigenvalues $\frac{3-1}{2} = 1$ and $\frac{0-1}{2} = -\frac12$ (twice). By Rayleigh's principle the maximum is $1$, attained at $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1)$, and the minimum is $-\frac12$, attained at any unit vector with $x + y + z = 0$, for instance $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$.

Equivalently, for all real $x, y, z$,
$$-\tfrac12(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) \le xy + yz + zx \le x^2 + y^2 + z^2.$$
Both are classical olympiad inequalities, usually proved from $(x - y)^2 + (y - z)^2 + (z - x)^2 \ge 0$ and $(x + y + z)^2 \ge 0$. The eigenvalue method explains where these sums of squares come from and why the constants are sharp.

blocks.title: Symmetric roots of the identity
blocks.body: Let $A$ be a real symmetric matrix with $A^k = I$ for some $k \ge 1$. Prove that $A^2 = I$.
blocks.solution:
Write $A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. Then $A^k = QD^kQ^{\mathsf T} = I$ gives $D^k = Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$, so every eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda^k = 1$. The eigenvalues are real, and the only real $k$-th roots of unity are $\pm1$, so $\lambda^2 = 1$ for every eigenvalue. Hence $D^2 = I$ and $A^2 = QD^2Q^{\mathsf T} = QQ^{\mathsf T} = I$.

Without symmetry this fails: the rotation by $120^\circ$ satisfies $R^3 = I$ but $R^2 \ne I$. Its eigenvalues $e^{\pm 2\pi i/3}$ are not real, and that is exactly what the spectral theorem rules out.

blocks.body:
- The theorem needs symmetry, not just real eigenvalues. $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has real eigenvalues $1, 2$ and is diagonalisable, but its eigenvectors $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ are not perpendicular, so no orthogonal $Q$ works.
- Over $\mathbb C$ the right condition is Hermitian, not symmetric. The complex symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i\\ i & -1\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 = 0$ with $A \ne 0$, so it is not diagonalisable at all. More generally, a complex matrix $A$ can be written $A = UDU^{-1}$ with $U$ unitary and $D$ diagonal (now possibly with non-real entries) if and only if it is normal, $A\overline{A}^{\mathsf T} = \overline{A}^{\mathsf T}A$; we do not prove this here. Hermitian, real orthogonal and unitary matrices are normal.
- Eigenvectors for a repeated eigenvalue are not automatically orthogonal; orthogonalise inside each eigenspace.
- In a quadratic form $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$, the symmetric matrix has off-diagonal entries $b/2$, not $b$.
- $Q^{\mathsf T}AQ$ is diagonal; $QAQ^{\mathsf T}$ in general is not. Keep track of which way the change of basis goes.

Applying the spectral theorem to the symmetric matrix $A^{\mathsf T}A$ of an arbitrary matrix $A$ gives [[svd|the singular value decomposition]]. In several-variable calculus, the second-derivative test classifies a critical point by the eigenvalues of the symmetric Hessian matrix of [[partial-derivatives]], and maximising $x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ on the unit sphere is the model case of [[lagrange-multipliers]]: the multiplier is the eigenvalue.

Integer-valued versions of quadratic forms are the subject of [[quadratic-forms]], where orthogonal changes of variable are replaced by integer ones. The adjacency matrix of a graph is symmetric, and its eigenvalues bound the chromatic number and measure expansion ([[graph-basics]], [[graph-coloring]]). Random Hermitian matrices, and the spacings between their real eigenvalues, are the model behind [[pair-correlation]] for zeros of the zeta function. Infinite-dimensional versions, for self-adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces, underlie Fourier analysis ([[fourier-poisson]]) and quantum mechanics.

1. Orthogonally diagonalise $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4\\ 4 & -3\end{pmatrix}$ and describe the map geometrically.
2. Show that $A^{\mathsf T}A$ is symmetric with non-negative eigenvalues for every real matrix $A$.
3. Find the maximum of $x^2 + 4xy + y^2$ on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.
4. Show that a real symmetric matrix with all eigenvalues in $\{0, 1\}$ is the orthogonal projection onto a subspace.
